On the first warm Saturday in March, my neighbor takes his kitchen chairs outside and washes them on the pavement. He uses a yellow bucket, a square of old towel, and a toothbrush for the places where the spindles meet the seat. By noon the chairs are standing in a row against the brick wall, looking like a small audience waiting for something to begin.

Last year I asked why he did it outside. There was hardly room in his kitchen, he said. Then he admitted that he liked the company. Sure enough, people stopped. A cyclist asked for directions. Two girls counted the chairs in French. A woman coming home with groceries put down her bags and told him her father had owned a set exactly like them, except that one leg had been mended with a spoon.

I thought about that spoon all afternoon. Had somebody flattened it first? Was the bowl still visible? I hoped so. It pleased me to imagine a family eating supper for years above one extra spoon, promoted from the drawer to a position of considerable responsibility.

This morning the yellow bucket appeared again. I took my cup of coffee downstairs and sat on the step. My neighbor handed me the toothbrush without a word. We worked on opposite sides of a chair until a little boy in a green coat stopped to watch.

“Which one is the cleanest?” he asked.

We looked along the row. Neither of us had thought to keep track.
